questions.prompt: What is the pressure-volume work done by a gas during a constant-volume process?
questions.answer:
Pressure-volume work is
\[
W=\int p\,dV
\]
For a constant-volume process, \(dV=0\), so
\[
W=0
\]

questions.prompt: A gas expands at constant pressure \(1.5\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) by \(0.020\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find \(W\).
questions.answer:
For constant pressure,
\[
W=p\Delta V
\]
\[
W=(1.5\times10^5)(0.020)=3.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}
\]
The gas expands, so the work is positive.

questions.prompt: A gas is compressed at constant pressure \(2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) from \(0.050\) to \(0.030\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find \(W\).
questions.answer:
The volume change is
\[
\Delta V=0.030-0.050=-0.020\,\mathrm{m^3}
\]
At constant pressure,
\[
W=p\Delta V
\]
\[
W=(2.0\times10^5)(-0.020)=-4.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}
\]
The negative sign shows compression.

questions.prompt: A gas pressure varies linearly from \(1.0\times10^5\) to \(3.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) while volume increases from \(0.020\) to \(0.050\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find the work done by the gas.
questions.answer:
For a linear pressure change, the work is the average pressure times the volume change:
\[
W=\frac{p_i+p_f}{2}(V_f-V_i)
\]
\[
W=\frac{1.0\times10^5+3.0\times10^5}{2}(0.050-0.020)
\]
\[
W=(2.0\times10^5)(0.030)=6.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}
\]

questions.prompt: A gas expands with pressure \(p(V)=aV\), where \(a=4.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{Pa\,m^{-3}}\), from \(V=0.010\) to \(0.030\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find \(W\).
A piston of area \(0.0040\,\mathrm{m^2}\) moves outward \(0.12\,\mathrm{m}\) against constant pressure \(1.8\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Find the work done by the gas.
questions.answer:
The volume change is piston area times displacement:
\[
\Delta V=A\Delta x
\]
\[
\Delta V=(0.0040)(0.12)=4.8\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}
\]
Then
\[
W=p\Delta V
\]
\[
W=(1.8\times10^5)(4.8\times10^{-4})=86.4\,\mathrm{J}
\]

questions.prompt: A gas follows \(p(V)=p_0(V_0/V)\) from \(V_0\) to \(3V_0\). Derive the work done by the gas.
Two processes connect the same volumes \(V_i\) and \(V_f\). One expands at high pressure \(p_h\), the other at low pressure \(p_l\). Which does more work and why?
questions.answer:
The high-pressure expansion does more work.

For expansion from \(V_i\) to \(V_f\),
\[
W=\int_{V_i}^{V_f}p\,dV
\]
The path with larger pressure at the same volumes has a larger area under the \(p\)-\(V\) curve, so it gives a larger positive work value.

questions.prompt: A gas expands from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\) along \(p=a+bV\), with \(a,b>0\). Derive \(W\), then state the condition for positive work.
questions.answer:
Use
\[
W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2}(a+bV)\,dV
\]
\[
W=a(V_2-V_1)+\frac{b}{2}(V_2^2-V_1^2)
\]
With \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and positive volumes, the work is positive for expansion:
\[
V_2>V_1
\]

questions.prompt: A rectangular cycle on a \(p\)-\(V\) diagram has corners \((V_1,p_1)\), \((V_2,p_1)\), \((V_2,p_2)\), and \((V_1,p_2)\), with \(V_2>V_1\) and \(p_2>p_1\). Derive the net work for clockwise and counterclockwise traversal.
questions.answer:
Only the horizontal parts contribute to \(p\,dV\); the constant-volume parts have \(dV=0\).

For clockwise traversal, expansion occurs at the higher pressure \(p_2\) and compression occurs at the lower pressure \(p_1\):
\[
W_{\mathrm{net}}=p_2(V_2-V_1)+p_1(V_1-V_2)
\]
\[
W_{\mathrm{net}}=(p_2-p_1)(V_2-V_1)
\]
For counterclockwise traversal, the sign reverses:
\[
W_{\mathrm{net}}=-(p_2-p_1)(V_2-V_1)
\]
